conversation.task: This is a fictional, low-stakes paper-collage rehearsal. A hobby club has twenty minutes, six circles, six rectangles, scrap paper, and pencils to draft one recognizable scene. A teammate says the first draft is confusing and proposes adding twelve tiny caption slogans to the small collage. You think those captions will make it hard to read. One imagined participant says a fast verbal explanation leaves them behind and asks for a written example. The group can try either a familiar town scene or a garden scene; both are reversible paper layouts. The known downside is that trying a second layout uses five of the twenty minutes. There is no evidence about which layout the group prefers. Nobody has proposed a process. Reply in English in no more than 250 words. Include a short welcoming opening, your response to the proposal and concern, a comparison of feasible approaches with one usable example, and a usable plan for this bounded session. Treat all advice as provisional for the fictional group to choose; do not execute anything.
conversation.response:
Welcome—there’s room to try a clear scene and hear everyone’s ideas.

The confusing first draft is useful feedback. I’d provisionally avoid twelve tiny slogans because they may crowd the small collage and compete with its shapes. The teammate may see a benefit I’m missing; they could explain what the captions would clarify. One short title is another option.

Assuming shapes can be moved and pencil details are allowed, these approaches use the same twenty minutes and available materials:

- **Town:** Use rectangles as buildings and circles as trees or wheels. Familiar outlines may help recognition, though crowded buildings could remain confusing.
- **Garden:** Use circles as flower heads and rectangles as beds or a path, with pencil stems. Repetition may look clear, though flowers might need details to distinguish them from other circles.
- **Compare both:** Spend five minutes trying the alternative layout. This offers direct evidence but leaves five fewer minutes for refinement.

Written example: “Garden: place three circles above three penciled stems. Put two rectangles below as planting beds. Leave space between them. Optional title: ‘Community Garden.’” Keep this visible and allow quiet reading before discussion.

Suggested session: minutes 0–3, read the example and invite preferences or concerns; 3–8, draft the group’s chosen scene; 8–13, either try the alternative or clarify the first; 13–18, choose and refine; 18–20, check recognizability and readability together. If preferences remain split, agree on a temporary choice while recording dissent. The fictional group makes the final decision.
